newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela prunes oil firm to grow new shoots.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela prunes oil firm to grow new shoots.

text.p: Restructuring at Venezuela's state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) will not only bring cost savings, but allow it to take advantage of more opportunities as the industry opens to private capital, analysts said on Tuesday.

In a letter to employees on Monday, PDVSA president Luis Giusti said he will dissolve PDVSA's three main subsidiaries, Maraven, Lagoven and Corpoven, to create three more focused business units. The vertically-integrated subsidiaries currently duplicate functions, while the new units will separate the upstream, downstream and other parts of the group.
The changes should generate savings of about $10 billion over 10 years, Giusti told journalists on Tuesday.

"The decision to restructure is a response to modern times. The organisation we had until now reflected the needs of other time... but we had to make way for new requirements of growing competition, adding value and improving coordination in the industry," he said.

Analysts said the change could be seen as PDVSA's coming of age, as it throws off the corporate structure inherited when the industry was nationalised in 1975. The new shape mirrors that of PDVSA's main rivals at the top of the oil world, such as Royal Dutch/Shell, Exxon and Saudi Arabia's Aramco.

"Every one else in the industry has been restructuring for the last five years... Now PDVSA is ending the illusion that its three main subsidiaries compete against each other," said Rafael Quijano, Latin America analyst for Petroleum Finance Corp in Washington.
Quijano agreed that savings would be substantial, but perhaps more importantly the company would be able to take decisions more easily and take advantage of more opportunities to expand.

"What they are doing is not just cutting costs, but making the organisation more efficient so they can do more business. PDVSA could make more money by pursuing opportunities than by cutting costs," he added.

With the sixth largest proven oil reserves in the world, and massive unproven deposits only beginning to be explored, PDVSA has embarked on a massive drive to increase production and open the industry to foreign capital.

Giusti played down the redundancies implied by the plan, but Quijano said that there would inevitably be some. However, the flood of foreign companies coming to the country would provide many new jobs for skilled people in the sector, he added.
The three new business units would be called PDV Exploration and Production, PDV Manufacturing and Supply, and PDV Services, Giusti's letter said.

The changes will begin in August this year with the link-up of the Cardon and Amuay refineries and should end by January next year. Together, the two plants will constitute the world's largest refinery with 940,000 barrels per day of capacity.

Oil and gas production would be the main concern of the PDV Exploration and Production, but it would also include a unit to manage joint-ventures in the largely unexploited Orinoco oil belt; Bitor, the boiler fuel maker; coal company Carbozulia; and CVP, which manages profit-sharing oil exploration contracts involving private capital.

PDV Manufacturing and Supply would cover refining; supply to the domestic market through Deltaven; international oil trading; shipping through PDV Marina; and the big U.S. subsidiary Citgo. It will also manage Pequiven, the state petrochemical group, although PDVSA is currently trying to persuade Congress to privatise it.
PDV Services will manage the other subsidiaries, such as Intesa, a technology affiliate; Palmaven, an agricultural supply company; and Bariven, a general materials supply firm.
